name: Pale Dull Glaucous-Blue
lede: Pale Dull Glaucous-Blue is a pale, slightly green-grey, built by putting the modifiers pale and dull in front of the base color [[glaucous-blue]], glaucous meaning the chalky blue-green bloom seen on grapes, plums and some leaves.

sections.title: Modifiers on a botanist's word
sections.body:
Pale Dull Glaucous-Blue stacks two modifier words, pale and dull, in front of the base color [[glaucous-blue]], in the compound-modifier grammar our library uses for names like this one [1]. *Glaucous* is an old botanical and zoological term for the waxy, frosted blue-green bloom on surfaces like a plum's skin or a eucalyptus leaf, and the base color carries that word into the color-naming systems [1]. Robert Ridgway first listed this swatch in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate XLII, hue 41, tone f, and the Inter-Society Color Council later filed it in the ISCC-NBS 1955 system as block 184 (R) [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[opal]], 4.0 units off, almost the same color on screen [2]; [[pale-russian-blue]] sits the same 4.0 units away [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within range of this swatch in 227 of 23,781 paintings, 0.95 percent, as photographed; looking for real coverage inside each painting narrows that to 166 [3]. That makes it more common than 68 percent of the named colors in our library [3]. It most often plays a light across its 166 appearances by lightness rank, so varnish cannot fake the result [3]. Alfred Sisley is its most devoted painter, present in 8 of his 50 works here, 9.0 times the expected rate for the museums those paintings come from [3].

The earliest match dates to 1445, nearly five hundred years before Ridgway's 1912 plate, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin; it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment or dye [3].
